Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
go along with whatever others want to feel safe

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette:
Rohan, a 41-year-old park ranger, found himself increasingly trapped by a past he desperately wished to outrun. His life had taken an irreversible turn nearly two years ago during a routine patrol in a secluded section of the national park. He had stumbled upon a makeshift camp, and before he could react, he was surrounded by a small, heavily armed group, dressed in mismatched military fatigues. They were poachers, he quickly realized, but their methods were chillingly organized, their demeanor menacing. For five harrowing days, Rohan was held captive, bound and interrogated, accused of spying, subjected to psychological intimidation and physical discomfort. He remembered the frightening event primarily as a series of stark, vivid pictures in his mind – a "snapshot memory" of the rough canvas tent, the glint of a knife, the faces of his captors. Sometimes, when these images flashed unbidden into his mind, he would feel a phantom "pain recall" in his wrists and ankles, where the ropes had chafed, or a dull ache in his jaw from a blow. Other times, the memory would surface with a chilling "emotionless recall," as if he were recounting a story that happened to a stranger, a detached narrative that felt profoundly unsettling.

Since his release, Rohan’s world had shrunk, governed by an invisible threat. He found his occupation, once a source of peace, now riddled with triggers. Any "talks about military" topics, whether from a visitor casually mentioning their service or a news report playing in the ranger station, would make his heart pound, a cold dread washing over him as if his captors were once again nearby. The sight of "people in uniform," even his own colleagues or a state trooper on patrol, sent a jolt of anxiety through him, a primal fear that authority could turn menacing at any moment. He was acutely aware of "being seen"; patrolling open trails or even sitting in his office with the blinds open made him feel exposed, vulnerable, constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats.

These triggers often brought on a terrifying sense of immediacy. A sudden rustle in the undergrowth or a hiker appearing quickly around a bend would cause him to "startle to movement," reacting as if in grave danger, his body tensing, ready to flee. At times, the past would overwhelm the present entirely; a particular scent or sound would plunge him into a "flashback," suddenly feeling and acting as if he were back in that damp, claustrophobic tent, the terror palpable and all-consuming. Despite his partner, Priya, repeatedly assuring him of his safety at home, he found it "impossible to believe" her, his mind always anticipating danger, checking locks, peering out windows, unable to truly relax.

Internally, Rohan was consumed by a profound sense of "humiliation" over what had happened, a feeling that he had been utterly powerless and exposed. This led to a harsh "self-comparison"; he was certain that "somebody else would not have gotten into this situation," blaming himself for not being more vigilant, stronger, or smarter. This self-reproach fed into a deep sense of "isolation," making him feel profoundly "set apart from others," convinced no one could truly understand the shame or the constant vigilance he endured.

To cope, Rohan developed a series of maladaptive strategies. He began to "restrict eating," meticulously counting calories and sometimes skipping meals, finding a strange, albeit fleeting, sense of control in managing his food intake – a stark contrast to the utter lack of control he had experienced during captivity. At night, he would lie awake, consumed by "revenge fantasies" against his captors, imagining elaborate scenarios where he regained his power and exacted justice. These thoughts were dark and exhausting but offered a temporary, potent release from his feelings of helplessness. In his interactions, especially at work or with people he perceived as powerful, he became overtly agreeable, often engaging in "people pleasing," going along with whatever others wanted to "feel safe" and avoid conflict.

Over the months, these patterns took a heavy toll. His "restrict eating" left him constantly fatigued, making the physical demands of his park ranger duties increasingly difficult. His "people pleasing" meant he was overworked, taking on extra shifts and tasks to avoid confrontation, leaving him little time for himself or Priya. The "isolation" he felt, despite living with Priya, created a growing chasm between them, as he struggled to articulate the depths of his internal suffering, convinced she wouldn't understand his profound humiliation.

The breaking point arrived when a minor dispute with a group of campers escalated. Rohan, paralyzed by his "people pleasing" tendencies and the fear of confrontation, froze, unable to assert his authority effectively. The incident led to a formal complaint and a stern warning from his supervisor. Priya, noticing his increasing withdrawal, his erratic eating habits, and the dark circles under his eyes, gently but firmly suggested he seek help. He finally understood he couldn't continue living this way, haunted by his past, always on edge. He came to therapy hoping to find a way to reclaim his life, but what frightened him most was the lingering certainty that he might never truly feel safe again, that the humiliation would forever define him.
